00 - Course Overview and Note Index

The Nature of Mind · UC Berkeley Philosophy 3 — Course Overview and Note Index

The course is officially titled Philosophy 3: The Nature of Mind. It was taught in the Fall 2014 semester (FL14) by John Campbell in the UC Berkeley Department of Philosophy, MWF 2–3, in room 2 LeConte. The videos were uploaded to YouTube by CosmoLearning, and the 27 notes in this directory correspond one-to-one with the 27 videos in the playlist.

• Playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLWhEiaivg3MaODGDb23kp_O2lGswTVgHZ

• Syllabus (archived page of the Berkeley Department of Philosophy): https://philosophy.berkeley.edu/courses/detail/778

Editions. This is the English edition. Its Chinese sibling lives one level up, in Phil3-Nature-of-Mind/ (index: 00 - 课程总览与笔记索引.md). The [[wikilinks]] in the lecture table below deliberately point at the Chinese filenames, so they resolve inside that edition; within this folder the English files carry the identical names, so 06 - Ned Block's Troubles with Functionalism resolves here too.

• Assigned texts: Philosophy of Mind: Classical and Contemporary Readings, edited by David Chalmers; and Personal Identity, edited by John Perry (in class these are often transcribed as "the Chalmers collection" and "the Perry collection")

Course Structure (the five syllabus units)

The syllabus divides the course into five segments, and the ordering of this note set follows it:

Unit

Lectures

Main thread

Foundations

01–04

dualism, behaviorism, central state materialism

Functionalism

05–10

Putnam's functionalist hypothesis, Block's internal criticism, the inverted spectrum, Searle's Chinese room

Consciousness

11–17

Nagel's bat, approaches to and discussion of the science of consciousness, Jackson's Mary, Huxley's automata, schizophrenia, imagination and physicalism

Personal Identity

18–23

three lectures on Locke, Williams, and Parfit

Intentionality

24–27

Churchland's eliminativism, Dennett's intentional strategy, Clark & Chalmers' extended mind, final review

Three Important Notes About the Source Material

1. The playlist has two titles attached to the wrong videos, and one title that does not match its content. The YouTube title of lecture 08 is Searle's Can Computers Think?, but the video actually presents Nagel on brain bisection and the unity of consciousness (the framing sections on Searle are merged into lecture 09 along with the Chinese room). The title of lecture 20 is "Review for Exam 2", but the recording is in fact a close reading of Locke's Of Identity and Diversity and Williams' The Self and the Future, not a survey of lectures 11–19. The title of lecture 19 is Williams' The Self and the Future, but the content of the recording is free will and autonomy. The filenames of the three notes keep the original playlist titles (so that they can be matched against the videos), while the body text and the frontmatter are both written according to what the recording actually contains, and the mismatch is flagged prominently inside those notes.

2. Lecture 19 has no English subtitles; its note comes from a fresh transcription. For that video only a badly corrupted Spanish auto-caption track survives on YouTube (442 segments, about 965 words, semantically unusable). The note was therefore re-transcribed instead from a recording of the same lecture on the Internet Archive (item ucberkeley_webcast_bwayUqZLwRo, 2014-11-19) using Whisper base.en, so the wording, punctuation, and spelling of proper names in that lecture differ in source from the other lectures; every quotation has been checked back one by one.

3. All the original transcripts are inside the _work/ directory and are available for verification.

• _work/clean/<video_id>.txt —— the cleaned English transcript of each lecture (no timestamps)

• _work/stamped/<video_id>.txt —— the same, in the [mm:ss] timestamped version

• _work/diag/L##_<video_id>.txt —— an index of paragraph start timestamps

• _work/diag/all_lectures.txt —— candidate proper names and rare words across all lectures (the basis for checking ASR corrections)

Shared Structure of the Lecture Notes

Every note contains nine sections: Chapter Overview (a timestamp navigation table) → Overall Summary (about 400 words, with "the points most worth attention") → Topic Chapters (4–8 themes, each with 3–5 bullet points) → Key Quotes (10–15 verbatim English sentences, each with its Chinese context) → Novel Ideas → Counter-intuitive Views → Core Tensions → Methodology → Key Data.

The notes observe two disciplines: write only what actually occurs in the recording (do not smuggle in the standard textbook readings of Descartes, Putnam, or Parfit), and do not use attribution prefixes such as "he says" or "the speaker thinks" (views are stated directly, since the speaker is already identified in the frontmatter). Quotations preserve the original spelling of the auto-captions, and errors that are phonetically close have been corrected in context in the Chinese narration.
